first_impression: I'd definitely click on this on itch or Steam because the cozy Scottish pastoral theme and the warm sunset palette look great. Then I look closer at the actual in-game screenshots and it's clear the low-poly art style is pretty barebones and flat. The premise of playing an actual working border collie with classic trials and wolf defense is brilliant though.
best_things: The UI and typography are exceptionally clean, warm, and readable, looking like a finished, high-end indie title right away.
Every single level introduces a genuine mechanical twist - from stubborn rams and vulnerable lambs to full-on sheepdog trial courses and weather hazards.
The charm loadout system tied to star collection gives a tangible mechanical reason to master each evening rather than just checking off a level.

worst_problems.problem: The camera angle in e1-low-view.jpg completely obscures the dog and sheep behind huge clunky low-poly pine tree foliage, ruining visibility.
worst_problems.suggestion: Dithering or cutouts on foreground trees are mandatory if the camera swings low, otherwise you are playing blind.

worst_problems.problem: The environment texture and terrain mesh look very flat and primitive compared to the polished UI, especially the bare stretches of yellow-green grass and basic river geometry.
worst_problems.suggestion: Add more varied ground scatter, depth to water edges, and better soft shading to stop it from looking like a default Unity terrain prototype.

worst_problems.problem: The sheep models are extremely blocky and rigid polygonal wedges with no apparent fleece fluffiness or expressive bounce when moving.
worst_problems.suggestion: Give sheep slightly softer silhouette curves and strong squash-and-stretch or bobbing animations so herding them feels lively and tactile.

worst_problems.problem: The wolf stalking UI warning and the dashed detection rings look a bit too clinical and gamey, breaking the serene countryside atmosphere.
worst_problems.suggestion: Rely more on sound cues, subtle vignetting, and natural wolf posture instead of bright dashed circles and red targeting lines.

worst_problems.problem: The minimap styling is stark and looks like a schematic vector drawing rather than fitting the beautiful vintage font and card design of the rest of the game.
worst_problems.suggestion: Make the map look like an ink-and-watercolor hand-drawn shepherd's sketch or parchment map to match the cozy storybook theme.

boredom_points: Circling endlessly around stubborn single sheep when their turning radius doesn't cooperate, especially with a slow-paced creep mechanic.
Replaying levels just to chase pure completionist ribbons without unlocking brand new gameplay mechanics.
confusions: Why the dog is suddenly crouching directly under pine branches in e1-low-view.jpg - is that a specific stealth ambush mechanic or just awkward camera collision?
Whether barking actually hurts or only alerts wolves, since the tooltips only mention sheep fleeing and rams needing a stare-down or bark.
wish_list: A free-roam endless shepherd mode where you just tend the flock across hills without timer pressure.
Whistle commands from the farmer that you have to respond to for extra trial authenticity.
Visual customization for Pip, like collars or bandanas unlocked with ribbons alongside the charms.
one_line_review: A surprisingly smart and authentic sheepdog sim wrapped in a lovely UI, held back only by slightly stiff low-poly visuals.
